When two conclusions appear to agree, the system compares their full justification graphs (including defeaters, undercutters, and evidence nodes). If the graphs are isomorphic, the conclusions are merged; otherwise, they remain distinct even if the conclusions are logically equivalent.", "scope": {"covers": ["argumentation-based reasoning systems", "systems with explicit evidential reasoning and defeaters"], "excludes": ["systems without argumentation structures", "black-box neural systems"]}, "forbidden": [{"case": "Two conclusions with isomorphic justification graphs are merged, but one graph contains a subtle defeater that is dormant in the current context. When the context changes, the defeater activates for the merged conclusion, but the system cannot distinguish which original conclusion is undermined, leading to wholesale rejection of the merged belief.", "eval": "program:defeater_activation_audit"}, {"case": "The system fails to merge two conclusions that are semantically identical but have non-isomorphic justification graphs due to different evidential paths, leading to belief fragmentation and contradictory updates when new evidence arrives.", "eval": "program:belief_fragmentation_detector"}], "prose_notes": "This criterion is too strict: it demands structural identity of justifications, which can prevent merging of genuinely identical claims reached via different evidential routes. It also risks merging claims that are only superficially similar in justification but differ in subtle, context-dependent ways."}
